A term with v ≥ 3 gives a^3 divisible by 3^9, hence ≡ 0 (mod 3^7). So such entries do not obstruct divisibility by 3^7.

We now count ordered triples (a,b,c) by the minimum 3-adic valuation m of their cubes (m ∈ {0,3,6,≥9}). If m ≥ 9 (i.e. all three a,b,c have v ≥ 3) then each cube is ≡ 0 (mod 3^7), so every such triple works. The number of such triples is 27^3 = 19683.

If m = 6 (so the minimum v is 2), then every v = 2 term contributes 3^6·(unit) and every v ≥ 3 term contributes 0 (mod 3^7), and units are ±1 mod 3. Working modulo 3 we find that exactly those triples with either exactly two v=2 entries whose unit-cubes are opposite modulo 3, or all three v=2 with all three unit-cubes equal, give total sum ≡ 0 (mod 3^7). Counting these gives
- r = 2 (exactly two entries v=2): 3 choices of which two positions × (2·27·27 choices to make the two units opposite mod 3) × 27 choices for the remaining (v ≥ 3) = 118098,
- r = 3 (all three v=2): 2·27^3 = 39366.
Total for m = 6: 157464.

Summing the three nonzero contributions we get
19683 + 157464 + 354294 = 531441 = 3^12.
